usage: exactly 12:00 in the daytime, no 시 needed
무렵 = 'around the time of', softens the exactness
examples: 에 attaches straight to 정오 — never 정오에 시
정오 is the word announcements and schedules use
부터 marks the starting point of an event
nuance: 정오 is Sino-Korean 正午 ('exact' 正 + 'the horse hour' 午, the old zodiac slot for midday), so it literally pins down 12:00 in the daytime with a crisp, official feel. The everyday spoken equivalent is 낮 12시, which is what friends actually say; 정오 belongs to schedules, broadcasts, train timetables and writing. Do not confuse it with plain 낮, which is the whole bright part of the day, not the single instant — 정오 is one point, 낮 is a span. The big English-speaker pitfall is treating it like the clock reading and tacking on 시: there is no 정오 시. Just say 정오 by itself, or switch to 낮 12시 if you want the casual register. Its mirror-image partner is 자정 (midnight, 12 a.m.).

usage: exactly 12:00 at night, the day's turning point
examples: I go to bed at midnight.
자정 is standard in deadlines and notices
자정이 넘다 = the clock has gone past 12
nuance: 자정 is Sino-Korean 子正 ('the rat hour' 子, the zodiac slot straddling midnight + 'exact' 正), naming the precise instant the date flips from one day to the next. It is the clean single-word counterpart of 정오 (noon); together they form the noon/midnight pair. In casual speech people say 밤 12시, but for cut-offs, deadlines and announcements 자정 is the standard term. Beware two English-speaker traps: first, do not stretch 자정 to mean 'late at night' in general — that vague 'middle of the night' feeling is 한밤중, while 자정 is the exact 12:00 point. Second, like 정오 it takes no 시 (never 자정 시). And remember it signals a.m.: anything just after 자정 belongs to the new day, which is why the dark hours that follow are called 새벽.

english: dawn, the small hours (early morning before sunrise)
usage: roughly 1 a.m. to just before sunrise
at dawn / in the small hours
새벽 + native-number hour pins it to the a.m. side
examples: 에 marks the time you woke
I caught a flight at 4 a.m.
새벽 + hour tells the listener it's a.m., not p.m.
I worked until the small hours last night.
까지 = until; note Korean uses 새벽, English says 'last night'
nuance: 새벽 is a native Korean word for the dark stretch from roughly 1 a.m. to just before sunrise, the slot that comes after 자정 (midnight) and before 아침 (morning proper, after the sun is up). Its job in real speech is to disambiguate the clock: Korean has no a.m./p.m. tags, so 새벽 4시 tells the listener you mean 4 in the morning, not the afternoon. Contrast it with 아침: 아침 7시 feels like the start of a normal day, whereas 새벽 5시 feels strikingly early or like you never slept. Note a culture-of-language pitfall: Koreans count these pre-sunrise hours as belonging to the previous night, so 'I stayed up till 3 last night' is 어제 새벽 3시까지 — the date logic differs from English. Also pair 새벽 with native-number hours (새벽 다섯 시), and never assume it could mean p.m.

english: midday, the middle of the day (broad daylight)
usage: the brightest, hottest stretch around noon
in the middle of the day
의 links 한낮 to the following noun
examples: It's too hot in the middle of the day.
는 adds topic/contrast to the 에 phrase
한낮의 + noun is a stock descriptive pairing
Even though it was broad daylight, the street was dark.
한낮 used for vivid contrast with the gloom
nuance: 한낮 is native Korean: the intensifier 한- ('the very peak of', the same 한 in 한가운데 'dead center') fused with 낮 ('daytime'), so it means the very middle of the day, around noon, when the sun is highest and strongest. The dividing line versus plain 낮 is intensity and focus: 낮 is the whole daytime span and is neutral, while 한낮 zooms in on the peak hours and almost always carries a vivid sensory charge — heat, glare, stillness. That is why it collocates so naturally with 더위 (heat), 햇볕 (sunlight) and 땡볕 (blazing sun). The English-speaker pitfall is using 한낮 as a generic 'in the daytime'; for that everyday sense just say 낮에. Reserve 한낮 for when you really mean high noon at its brightest or hottest. Its night-time mirror is 한밤중 (the dead of night).

english: the middle of the night, the dead of night
usage: in the middle of the night
even in the dead of night
도 = even, stressing the unlikely hour
examples: A call came in the middle of the night.
한밤중 frames it as an inconvenient hour
I suddenly woke up in the dead of night.
갑자기 = suddenly; pairs with the eerie tone
The shop is open even in the dead of night.
도 stresses how surprising the late opening is

Set it against plain 밤, which is simply 'night' as a neutral span; 한밤중 zooms in on the dead-quiet core and almost always carries an extra colour of 'an unusual, inconvenient, or eerie hour'. That is why it loves verbs of disturbance — 전화가 오다 (a call comes), 깨다 (wake up), 깜짝 놀라다 (be startled). Unlike 자정 it is not a precise clock point: 자정 is exactly 12:00, while 한밤중 is a fuzzy 'somewhere in the dead of night'. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for it to mean 'late evening' — at 9 or 10 p.m. you would just say 밤; save 한밤중 for the genuinely deep, silent hours.

usage: 는 marks topic/contrast with other years
안에 = within, before the year is out
examples: I came to Korea this year.
no 에 — 올해 sits straight before the verb
는 contrasts it with calmer years
I want to graduate within this year.
올해 안에 = before this year ends
nuance: 올해 is the native Korean word for the present calendar year and slots straight in front of a verb, normally WITHOUT 에: 올해 졸업해요 (I graduate this year), not 올해에. It anchors the three-year set 작년 (last year) – 올해 (this year) – 내년 (next year). There is a Sino-Korean synonym 금년 (今年, 'present year'), but it is stiff and limited to formal writing or speeches; in conversation 올해 is the only natural choice. Two English-speaker pitfalls stand out. First, the 에 habit: because English says 'in this year' learners over-add 에, but native usage drops it after 올해. Second, the look-alike trap with 오늘 ('today') — both start with 오, yet 올해 is a whole year and 오늘 is a single day, so 'I'm twenty this year' is 올해 스무 살이에요, never 오늘.

Confusing 올해 (this year) with 오늘 (today) — same 오- start, but one is a year and one is a day.

usage: the year just before this one
에 is the natural particle for this past time point
examples: I came to Korea last year.
작년 takes 에 — unlike 올해, which drops it
작년 + season = a specific past season
I've been learning Korean since last year.
부터 marks the start of an ongoing action
nuance: 작년 is Sino-Korean 昨年 ('past/previous' 昨, the same 昨 in 작일 'yesterday' + 'year' 年), so it literally means 'the previous year'. Crucially, unlike 올해, it normally DOES take 에 when used as a time point: 작년에 만났어요 (we met last year). It is the everyday word; the synonym 지난해 ('the year that passed') is a touch more formal and common in news writing, while 작년 dominates conversation. It completes the set 작년 – 올해 – 내년. Watch two English-speaker pitfalls. First, mirroring 올해's no-particle habit and dropping 에 — for past-time 작년, 에 is the natural marker. Second, the look-alike 작년/어제: both involve 'past', but 작년 is a whole year back and 어제 is just yesterday, so 'I arrived last year' is 작년에, never 어제.

mistakes: Dropping 에 in time-point sentences — say 작년에 갔어요; bare 작년 갔어요 sounds incomplete here, unlike 올해.

usage: the year just after this one
에 is the natural particle for this future time point
examples: I'm going to Korea next year.
내년 takes 에 like 작년, unlike 올해
졸업하다 = to graduate; 에 marks the future point
내년 초 = the start of next year + 에
nuance: 내년 is Sino-Korean 來年 ('to come' 來 + 'year' 年), literally 'the coming year'. Like its opposite 작년, it normally takes 에 as a time point: 내년에 시작해요 (it starts next year). It rounds out the trio 작년 – 올해 – 내년. There is a more literal native phrasing 다음 해 ('the next year'), but 내년 is the compact everyday word; 다음 해 surfaces mainly when contrasting several years in a row. Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, the same 에 issue as 작년 — for future-time 내년, 에 is the natural marker, so don't strip it the way you would after 올해. Second, the dangerous look-alike 내년/내일: both start with 내- and both point forward, but 내년 is a whole year ahead while 내일 is just tomorrow, so 'I'll graduate next year' is 내년에, and saying 내일 would promise something a year too soon.

usage: set phrase; 종일 = the whole day through
examples: I want to rest just one day.
I take the medicine three times a day.
하루에 marks the rate, not a point in time
하루 종일 = the whole day long, a fixed phrase
nuance: 하루 is the native Korean word for a single 24-hour day and lives inside several fixed phrases you should memorise as chunks: 하루 종일 (all day long), 하루에 ... 번 (... times a day), and the doubled 하루하루 (day by day, one day at a time). Here 하루 is pure native counting, which is why it heads the irregular native day-count series 하루(1)·이틀(2)·사흘(3)·나흘(4) rather than taking 일(日) the way calendar dates do. Two English-speaker pitfalls. First, the rate construction: 'once a day' is 하루에 한 번, with 에 carrying the 'per' meaning — never 하루 번. Second, do not let 하루 drift into meaning 'today'; 하루 is 'a day' as a length or an unspecified day ('one day...'), whereas 'today' is the separate word 오늘. So 'I worked all day today' combines both: 오늘 하루 종일 일했어요.

english: a few days; what date / which day
usage: 며칠 here asks the calendar number
examples: I met a friend a few days ago.
며칠 전에 = a few days back
the set way to ask the day-of-month number
I rested well for a few days.
며칠 동안 = over the span of several days
nuance: 며칠 carries two everyday senses decided purely by context: the indefinite 'a few days' (며칠 동안 쉬었어요 = I rested for a few days) and the question 'what date' (오늘 며칠이에요? = what's today's date?). The single most important point for any learner — native or foreign — is the spelling: it is ALWAYS 며칠, never 몇일. Even though 'how many' is 몇 and 'day' is 일(日), the fused word lost that shape and is written 며칠 by rule, so 몇일 is simply a misspelling. Mind the boundary with two neighbours: 며칠 asks the date (a number, 17th), whereas 무슨 요일 asks the day of the week (Monday, Tuesday), and 얼마나 asks 'how long'. So if you want 'which weekday is it', do not say 며칠 — use 무슨 요일이에요? Tone and the surrounding words tell a listener instantly whether you are estimating a span or asking the calendar.

usage: a moment both speakers already know
그때 + 그 + noun, e.g. 그때 그 사람
examples: Back then I was a student.
는 frames that period as the topic/contrast
그때 reused for an agreed FUTURE time
nuance: 그때 is the demonstrative 그 ('that', the listener-known one) fused with 때 ('time, occasion'), so it points at a specific moment both speakers can already identify — looking back ('back then') or to a plan just arranged ('see you then'). Write it solid as 그때; the spaced 그 때 is non-standard. Mind the demonstrative trio that mirrors 이/그/저: 이때 = this moment / now in the flow of events, 그때 = that known moment, and the question 언제 = 'when?'. The key English-speaker pitfall is the 'that' default: because English freely says 'that time' for brand-new information, learners reach for 그때 even when the listener has no idea which moment is meant. But 그때 presupposes shared knowledge — if the time is new to your listener you must first establish it (give the date or event), and only then can 그때 refer back to it.

structuredNuance.t: 그때 points at a specific moment both speakers can already identify — looking back ('back then') or to a plan just arranged ('see you then'). Write it solid as 그때; the spaced 그 때 is non-standard.
Mind the demonstrative trio that mirrors 이/그/저: 이때 = this moment / now in the flow of events, 그때 = that known moment, and the question 언제 = 'when?'.
그때 is the demonstrative 그 ('that', the listener-known one) fused with 때 ('time, occasion').

The key English-speaker pitfall is the 'that' default: because English freely says 'that time' for brand-new information, learners reach for 그때 even when the listener has no idea which moment is meant. But 그때 presupposes shared knowledge — if the time is new to your listener you must first establish it (give the date or event), and only then can 그때 refer back to it.

mistakes: Writing it as two words 그 때 — the standard spelling is the single word 그때.
Using 그때 for a brand-new time the listener can't yet identify — 그때 needs a shared, already-known moment.
Confusing 그때 (that known time) with 이때 (this/now) or 언제 (when?) — the 이/그/저 logic still applies.

usage: rare 나중 without 에, here object of 위해
examples: -ㄹ게요 = a friendly promise to do it
polite way to postpone a topic
맨 나중에 = at the very end of the sequence
nuance: 나중 is the native noun for a later, unspecified time, and in practice it is almost fused with its particle: you will hear 나중에 ('later, afterward') far more than bare 나중. It is the go-to word for gently postponing things — 나중에 이야기해요 (let's talk later), 나중에 봐요 (see you later). The crucial dividing lines are with two near-synonyms. 이따가 means 'in a little while', but specifically LATER THE SAME DAY, a short wait; 나중에 is open-ended and can be days, months, or a vague someday. 다음에 means 'next time', tied to the next occasion or meeting rather than just elapsed time. So 'see you later today' leans 이따가 봐요, 'see you next time' is 다음에 봐요, and the all-purpose vague 'later' is 나중에 봐요. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the particle (bare 나중 sounds incomplete) and over-using 나중에 for the same-day 'in a bit', where 이따가 is more precise.
